content: 1. Warders or other transport operators provide guidance to the sender regarding the required shipping documents and instructions for their completion. 2. They advise the sender on the appropriate packaging for the materials being shipped. 3. They assist the sender in determining the most direct routing for the shipment and confirm the routing once finalized. 4. They maintain and archive copies of all documentation related to the shipment and transport, such as importation permits, which may need to be provided to the sender when applicable. 5. They arrange for the most timely and efficient collection of the shipment upon arrival. 6. They acknowledge receipt of the shipment to the sender. 7. Before offering a consignment of dangerous goods for transport, all individuals involved in its preparation must receive adequate training to fulfill their responsibilities. 8. If the organization responsible for preparing the shipment lacks appropriately trained personnel, the term relevant persons may include those contracted to act on behalf of the shipper and undertake the shipper's responsibilities. These individuals must still meet applicable training requirements. 9. Personnel should be trained in alignment with their contractual responsibilities, and the training content should be based on an analysis of their assigned roles and duties as outlined in their job descriptions. 10. In some cases, the employer determines the training requirements, while in others, these are stipulated or governed by national competent authorities. 11. Employees should only perform functions for which they have received the required training. Otherwise, they must be appropriately supervised and signed off by a competent individual. 12. According to UN model regulations, all individuals involved in the transport of dangerous goods must be trained in general awareness and familiarization, safety, and specific functions. 13. General awareness and familiarization training should include knowledge of the general provisions of dangerous goods transport requirements, such as: Description of the classes of dangerous goods. Labeling, marking, and placarding. Packaging requirements. Segregation and compatibility of dangerous goods. Purpose and content of dangerous goods documentation. 14. A wide range of stakeholders must be appropriately trained for the safe and compliant shipment of infectious substances, including security personnel, freight forwarders, and designated postal operators. 15. The ICAO technical instructions provide a detailed overview of the various aspects of dangerous goods transport that personnel must be familiar with to be considered competent in shipping dangerous goods. 16. Function-specific training depends on the specific job functions of the individual. For example: A shipper at a public health institution may need training on classification, packing, labeling, marking, and documenting dangerous goods. A carrier may require training on handling, stacking, stowing, and logistics procedures. 17. Function-specific competencies should be supervised until competency is assured, which may require completing approved training courses or passing examinations. 18. Most modal agreements require testing and verification of an individual’s knowledge and competency in the aforementioned areas for anyone involved in dangerous goods transportation. 19. For example, UN model regulations mandate that individuals involved in the shipment of high-risk infectious substances (Category A) must undergo appropriate training and provide records of that training upon request. 20. Employers must maintain records of training conducted and make them available to employees or national competent authorities for verification, especially when individuals take on new responsibilities or appointments. 21. Training should be supplemented with retraining as deemed necessary by the competent authority, typically repeated every two years (24 months), though the frequency may vary depending on the mode of transport. 22. Training programs on dangerous goods may be subject to review and approval by relevant national competent authorities. 23. Before beginning the transportation process, it is essential to define what is being shipped and determine whether it qualifies as an infectious substance. 24. Cultures are concentrated collections of biological agents intentionally propagated under controlled laboratory conditions. Any cultured biological agent capable of causing disease in humans or animals is classified as an infectious substance. 25. Patient specimens, collected directly from humans or animals for research or diagnostic purposes, may also be classified as infectious substances if they contain biological agents capable of causing disease. 26. Biological products, such as antitoxins, vaccines, and vaccine components, may be subject to special requirements or licensing agreements due to their importance in disease treatment and prevention. 27. Live animals infected with biological agents must be transported in accordance with regulations in the country of origin, transit, and destination. Live animals must not be used as a means to transport biological agents unless no other measure is feasible. 28. Medical or clinical wastes contaminated with biological agents capable of causing disease are classified as infectious substances. 29. Medical devices or equipment contaminated with biological agents during patient treatment or laboratory processes may also be classified as infectious substances if the agents are capable of causing disease. 30. Exemptions may apply to certain materials, such as: Cultures of non-pathogenic biological agents. Patient specimens for specific diagnostic tests. Biological products like blood for transfusion or body parts for transplant. 31. Exempt specimens must be packaged using a basic triple packaging system, including a leak-proof primary receptacle, a leak-proof secondary packaging, and an outermost layer with adequate strength. 32. Infectious substances are classified based on their composition and the level of risk they pose to human or animal health. 33. Category A infectious substances are those that, when exposure occurs, can cause permanent disability, life-threatening, or fatal disease in otherwise healthy humans or animals. 34. Indicative lists of biological agents meeting the criteria for Category A are provided in transport regulations, though many agents only meet this definition when transported as cultures. 35. Category A infectious substances are assigned specific UN numbers and proper shipping names for transport purposes.
